subsection: 9. Northern Ireland during World War II and case study: Belfast during World War II

notes.b: Northern Ireland was part of the United Kingdom and fought in the war, so its industries and manpower were fully committed to the British war effort, in contrast to the neutral South.
points: Belfast's shipyards, chiefly Harland and Wolff, built warships and merchant ships for the Admiralty and the merchant fleet during the war.
Short Brothers at Belfast produced aircraft and aircraft parts, and the province's engineering works made munitions and military equipment.
The linen industry switched to producing military textiles, and agriculture in the north was expanded to feed the war effort.
Northern Ireland's neutrality was not an option: it was part of the United Kingdom, so the Stormont government took part in the war on Britain's side.
The war ended the Depression in Belfast's industries, and unemployment in the province fell sharply once war production began.

notes.b: Belfast was poorly protected against air raids. The city had few shelters and little air-raid planning when the bombing began in April 1941.
points: Before 1941 the city had limited shelter provision, many working-class houses had no shelter, and the air-raid services were under-resourced.
The Belfast city fire and rescue services were small, and the authorities depended on help from outside the city when raids came.
Belfast's blackout and warning arrangements were inadequate when the raids came in April 1941.

notes.h: The Belfast Blitz, April and May 1941
notes.b: German bombers attacked Belfast twice in the spring of 1941. The raids killed hundreds of people, destroyed much of the city's working-class housing, and exposed the poverty of the city's slums.
points: The first raid took place on 15–16 April 1941, when German bombers attacked the city's docks, the Harland and Wolff shipyard and the shipping and industrial areas.
The second raid, on 4–5 May 1941, was heavier: it hit the city centre and the working-class districts, and it was followed by fires that spread through many streets.
About 900 people were killed in the two raids, and thousands were injured and left homeless, though casualty figures vary between sources.
Thousands of houses were destroyed or damaged, and many families who lost their homes were moved to temporary housing on the edges of the city.
Fire brigades from Dublin, and from other parts of Ireland, travelled north to help fight the fires, a notable act of cross-border assistance.
The bombing revealed the shortage of decent housing in Belfast's slums, where many families lived in overcrowded terraces without basic sanitation.

notes.b: Evacuation moved children and families out of the city after the raids. It exposed the condition of the working poor and their children.
points: Children and families were evacuated from Belfast to rural areas after the raids, and host families were often unprepared for the children's poor health and clothing.
The evacuation exposed the scale of poverty, malnutrition and disease among the city's working-class children, and it became a focus for social reform.
Many evacuees returned to Belfast once the immediate danger had passed, and the damaged housing they returned to became a political issue.

notes.h: Politics and government in the north, 1940–1945
notes.b: Northern Ireland's wartime government was led by Unionist prime ministers who coordinated the war effort with London and managed the province's industrial and social problems.
points: Sir John Miller Andrews was Prime Minister of Northern Ireland from 1940 to 1943, and he led the province through the Belfast Blitz.
Sir Basil Brooke succeeded Andrews as Prime Minister in 1943 and held office until 1963.
Unionist government ministers coordinated with London on war production and manpower, and the province's industrial strategy depended on British orders and funding.
Industrial unrest occurred during the war, and strikes over wages and conditions in shipyards and factories were a regular feature of the period.

notes.h: American troops and the wider war effort
notes.b: American troops arrived in Northern Ireland in 1942, and their presence changed the social and economic life of the province.
points: American forces began to arrive in Northern Ireland in January 1942, and large numbers of US troops were stationed in the province before the invasion of Europe.
The presence of US troops brought new wealth, new social contact and tensions with local people, and it altered the social life of Belfast and the surrounding areas.
Northern Ireland provided bases and training grounds for Allied forces, and the province's ports and airfields were used for the Atlantic war and the preparation for D-Day.

notes.h: Social and political effects: housing, welfare and the Labour vote
notes.b: The war prompted social reform proposals, and the bombing made the case for new housing and welfare. Political debates in the province reflected the same pressures as in Britain.
points: The Beveridge Report of 1942, published in London, proposed a welfare system based on social insurance, and it influenced social debate in Northern Ireland.
The reconstruction of bombed housing became a major political question in Belfast, and the city's post-war housing programme was shaped by the damage of 1941.
Unionist governments kept the war effort central to their political appeal, presenting loyalty to Britain as the basis of the province's contribution to the war.

notes.b: Belfast in 1945 differed from 1939 in its damaged housing, its wartime industries and its larger US presence. It also remained divided on religious and political lines.
points: By 1945 many of the city's working-class districts had been damaged or rebuilt, and the physical landscape of Belfast had changed.
Wartime industry had expanded, and the city's economy had been revived by war production, though many of its pre-war industries remained in decline.
Sectarian and political divisions remained, and the Unionist government's control of the state continued unchanged through the war.

notes.h: Assessment: the war's effects on Northern Ireland
notes.b: Judgements of the war's effects depend on whether one measures change in economic recovery and social reform, or in continuing sectarian and political divisions.
points: Achievement: war production ended the Depression's worst effects and brought work to many of Belfast's unemployed.
Achievement: the bombing and evacuation pushed social reform and housing onto the political agenda, and Belfast's post-war reconstruction was partly a product of the Blitz.
Limit: the Unionist government continued to govern with the same structures, and the wartime period did not dismantle the Stormont system's discrimination.
Contemporary view: many contemporaries praised the war effort and the city's resilience during the bombing.
Later view: historians argue that the war was a turning point for Northern Ireland's social policy, but that its political divisions were not resolved by the war.
